title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
This exercise is my first end-to-end spatial workflow in R. I import polygon, line and point data, put every layer in a common projected coordinate reference system, and then use spatial relationships to answer two practical questions: how much land is covered by a cycling-path buffer in Tampines West, and how pre-school provision varies between subzones.






NoteData note



The lesson was originally written around KML and shapefile downloads. The current official portals provide GeoJSON, so I kept the analytical intention but used the live formats available in September 2026. Raw files are obtained by R/download-data.R and are not duplicated in the Git repository.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
1. Setup and data import
I first read one example of each geometry type. Looking at the geometry column separately from the attribute table helped me remember that an sf object is still a data frame; it simply carries a special list-column for shapes.

mpsz <- st_read(file.path(data_dir, "mp14-subzone.geojson"), quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_make_valid()

preschool <- st_read(file.path(data_dir, "preschools.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)
cycling <- st_read(file.path(data_dir, "cycling-paths.geojson"), quiet = TRUE)

tibble(
  layer = c("Subzones", "Pre-schools", "Cycling paths"),
  features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(preschool), nrow(cycling)),
  geometry = c(
    as.character(unique(st_geometry_type(mpsz))[1]),
    as.character(unique(st_geometry_type(preschool))[1]),
    as.character(unique(st_geometry_type(cycling))[1])
  ),
  crs = c(st_crs(mpsz)$input, st_crs(preschool)$input, st_crs(cycling)$input)
)

The default plot() method is useful as a quick diagnostic because it can show both the feature geometry and individual attributes. I use one attribute here to keep the result readable.

par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))
plot(st_geometry(mpsz), col = "#dce7f3", border = "#ffffff", main = "Geometry")
plot(mpsz["SUBZONE_N"], key.pos = NULL, reset = FALSE, main = "Attribute")
plot(st_geometry(mpsz), col = "#eef3f8", border = "#aebcd0", main = "Overlay")
plot(st_geometry(preschool), add = TRUE, pch = 20, cex = 0.25, col = "#d45b5b")

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
2. Coordinate reference systems
The imported files describe the same country but do not necessarily use the same CRS. Latitude/longitude is suitable for storage and web display; distance and area calculations need a projected CRS. I therefore transform every layer to SVY21 / Singapore TM (EPSG:3414).

crs_before <- tibble(
  layer = c("Subzones", "Pre-schools", "Cycling paths"),
  epsg = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(preschool)$epsg, st_crs(cycling)$epsg)
)

mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
preschool <- st_transform(preschool, 3414)
cycling <- st_transform(cycling, 3414)

crs_before

# A tibble: 3 × 2
  layer          epsg
  <chr>         <int>
1 Subzones       4326
2 Pre-schools    4326
3 Cycling paths  4326








TipMy check before analysis



st_set_crs() only changes the coordinate label. It does not move the geometry. Because these layers already have valid coordinates, st_transform() is the correct operation.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
section: 3. Converting Airbnb records to spatial points
text:
3. Converting Airbnb records to spatial points
The Airbnb file is an ordinary CSV. Its longitude and latitude columns become point geometry in WGS 84, after which I transform the points to EPSG:3414 for a valid overlay with the planning boundaries.

airbnb_raw <- read_csv(
  file.path(data_dir, "airbnb-listings.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

airbnb <- airbnb_raw |>
  filter(!is.na(longitude), !is.na(latitude)) |>
  st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(3414)

Airbnb listings over Master Plan 2014 subzones.




My first impression is that the listings are strongly clustered instead of being evenly distributed. The central area and several mature neighbourhoods stand out; that pattern would have been difficult to notice in the CSV alone.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
4. Five-metre cycling-path buffer
I select Tampines West, intersect the cycling lines with its boundary, and buffer the remaining lines by five metres. Summing every buffer polygon can double-count overlaps, so I dissolve them before calculating the final area.

tampines_west <- mpsz |>
  filter(SUBZONE_N == "TAMPINES WEST")

cycling_in_tampines <- st_intersection(cycling, tampines_west)
cycling_buffer <- st_buffer(cycling_in_tampines, dist = 5)
cycling_buffer_union <- st_union(cycling_buffer)

buffer_result <- tibble(
  measure = c("Sum before dissolving", "Dissolved footprint"),
  area_m2 = c(
    sum(as.numeric(st_area(cycling_buffer))),
    as.numeric(st_area(cycling_buffer_union))
  )
) |>
  mutate(area_km2 = area_m2 / 1e6)

buffer_result

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  measure               area_m2 area_km2
  <chr>                   <dbl>    <dbl>
1 Sum before dissolving 119204.    0.119
2 Dissolved footprint   106423.    0.106



ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = tampines_west, fill = "#eef3f8", colour = "#465d91") +
  geom_sf(data = cycling_buffer_union, fill = "#73c6b6", colour = NA, alpha = 0.85) +
  geom_sf(data = cycling_in_tampines, colour = "#24435d", linewidth = 0.35) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Cycling-path buffer", subtitle = "Tampines West, 5 metres") +
  theme_void()




Dissolved five-metre buffer around cycling paths in Tampines West.




The dissolved result is the more defensible estimate of land covered. The gap between the two numbers is a useful reminder that geometry overlaps are not just a display issue—they change summary statistics.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
5. Pre-school count and density
st_intersects() returns the pre-schools falling inside each subzone. I keep both the count and the density because they answer different questions: count describes total provision, while density adjusts for the physical size of the subzone.

mpsz_summary <- mpsz |>
  mutate(
    preschool_count = lengths(st_intersects(mpsz, preschool)),
    area_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6,
    preschool_density = preschool_count / area_km2
  )

highest_count <- mpsz_summary |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  slice_max(preschool_count, n = 5, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  select(SUBZONE_N, PLN_AREA_N, preschool_count, area_km2, preschool_density)

highest_count

       SUBZONE_N PLN_AREA_N preschool_count area_km2 preschool_density
1  TAMPINES EAST   TAMPINES              72 4.339828          16.59052
2 WOODLANDS EAST  WOODLANDS              54 2.553464          21.14775
3       ALJUNIED    GEYLANG              40 2.959367          13.51640
4  TAMPINES WEST   TAMPINES              38 3.475208          10.93460
5    BEDOK NORTH      BEDOK              38 3.203660          11.86143



ggplot(mpsz_summary) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = preschool_count), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.12) +
  geom_sf(data = preschool, colour = "#34495e", alpha = 0.45, size = 0.22) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "C", direction = -1) +
  coord_sf(datum = NA) +
  labs(title = "Pre-schools by subzone", fill = "Count") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(panel.grid = element_blank())




Pre-school locations and subzone-level counts.





density_data <- mpsz_summary |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  filter(is.finite(preschool_density))

p_hist <- ggplot(density_data, aes(preschool_density)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 25, fill = "#6f82aa", colour = "white") +
  labs(x = "Pre-schools per km²", y = "Subzones", title = "Density distribution") +
  theme_minimal()

p_scatter <- ggplot(
  density_data,
  aes(preschool_count, preschool_density)
) +
  geom_point(colour = "#465d91", alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, colour = "#d45b5b", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Pre-school count", y = "Pre-schools per km²", title = "Count versus density") +
  theme_minimal()

gridExtra::grid.arrange(p_hist, p_scatter, ncol = 2)




Distribution of density and the relationship between count and density.




The scatterplot confirms that a high count does not automatically imply the highest density. Small subzones can rank highly after area is taken into account. If I were extending this analysis, I would next relate provision to the number of young children rather than land area alone.

title: Hands-on Exercise 1A
text:
6. What I learned
Three checks made the workflow more reliable: inspect geometry and attributes before analysis, transform rather than relabel a valid CRS, and dissolve overlapping buffers before measuring area. The exercise also showed me why a map and a statistical plot should be read together—the map reveals geography, while the histogram and scatterplot reveal the shape of the values.
